name: New Incentives (charityevals estimate)
summary: New Incentives pays caregivers in northern Nigeria small cash incentives (up to ₦11,000 per child in 2024) when their infants receive routine vaccines at government clinics; in 2024 it enrolled 1.7 million infants in ten states at about $17 per infant. A randomised trial found the incentives raised full vaccination by 27 percentage points, and we combine that with Nigerian verbal-autopsy data on deaths from measles, pertussis, pneumococcus, Hib and rotavirus to estimate deaths averted. The bottom line is about 0.014 units of value per dollar, roughly 1.6 times GiveDirectly, with a very wide joint range (about 0.15 to 19 times). The biggest uncertainties are how many child deaths the extra vaccinations avert (cause-of-death data and vaccine efficacy) and how much of the trial's effect carries over to today's much larger program.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What New Incentives spent in 2024 (its audited financial year, ending 31 December), with management and fundraising spread over the program, and a small adjustment because part of the cost of infants enrolled in 2024 falls in 2025.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: Infants enrolled in 2024, from the charity's annual report. Each enrolled infant is followed through the routine schedule (birth to about 15 months), with a cash payment at each vaccination visit.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: Deaths averted per infant enrolled: the risk an unvaccinated child in the program area runs of dying before five from diseases the incentivised vaccines prevent, times the share of enrolled infants who get vaccinated only because of the incentive.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for how far the trial and cause-of-death evidence carry to the 2024 program, for vaccinations that would have happened later anyway, for the vaccines and clinic staff paid for by the government and Gavi, and for delivery falling short of reported enrolments.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: Deaths averted valued with GiveWell's moral weights, plus the value of the cash itself to poor households, and an allowance for benefits not modelled (illness averted, herd protection, vaccines given at the same visits).

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With salary sacrifice counted, your dollar is credited with its share only.

source.title: New Incentives and Subsidiary, audited consolidated financial statements, years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023
source.page: p. 5, Consolidated Statement of Activities, year ended December 31, 2024

rows.explainer: Program-service expenses for 2024, the same as the modelled program because New Incentives has a single program.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and general ($1.73 million) and fundraising ($0.13 million) over the program, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Cost of a full 2024 enrolment cohort relative to 2024 spending
rows.explainer:
An infant enrolled in 2024 keeps receiving payments (and staff visits) for up to about 15 months, so part of the 2024 cohort's cost is paid in 2025, while 2024 spending also covers the tail of the smaller 2023 cohort. The ₦5,000 completion incentive was introduced in 2024 (annual report, p. 4, "Introduced a completion incentive of ₦5,000"; New Incentives' history page dates it to July), so most completion payments for the 2024 cohort fall in 2025.

Best 1.15 is New Incentives' own cohort figure: "$17" per infant for 2024 (annual report, p. 21, total expenses ÷ infants, with completion incentives assigned to the cohort that earned them) against $14.81 from audited 2024 expenses ÷ 2024 enrolments. High 1.25: the audited statements' Note 8 shows net assets "Board designated for CCT commitments" rising from $4,427,720 to $10,230,006 during 2024, i.e. $5.8 million of payments promised to already-enrolled infants and not yet spent; audited spending plus that rise is $31.5 million, 1.23 × spending, close to the annual report's tentative $33.0 million of 2024 expenses. Low 1.05: part of that designation covers infants enrolled before 2024.

rows.label: Cost of the 2024 cohort, including overhead
rows.explainer: Audited 2024 spending with overhead, scaled to the full cost of the infants enrolled in 2024. Only New Incentives' own spending: the vaccines, cold chain and clinic staff are paid by the Nigerian government and Gavi and enter through the attribution share instead.

rows.label: Infants enrolled in 2024

source.title: New Incentives, Annual Report 2024
source.page: p. 8, 2024 Total Impact

rows.explainer: Infants newly enrolled in 2024 across 6,481 clinics in ten states (79% in North West states: Kano, Katsina, Jigawa, Sokoto, Kaduna, Kebbi, Zamfara; 21% in Bauchi and Gombe in the North East; a few in Niger State). This is the charity's administrative count; an infant is enrolled at the first incentivised vaccination. New Incentives' unannounced audits covered 13% of disbursement sessions. Independent coverage surveys measure coverage, not enrolment, so the count itself is not independently verified (see implementation_adj).

rows.label: Cost per infant enrolled
rows.explainer: About $17 per infant with the cohort adjustment ($14.81 on 2024 spending alone). New Incentives reports $17 for 2024 and $17.88 for 2023 (annual report, p. 21).

rows.label: Years at risk covered by the vaccines (first doses at 6 weeks to age 5)

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Appendix Table 2, note 7
source.quote: CSMR= (number of deaths by a specific cause/total number of live births) x 1,000

rows.explainer: The cause-specific death rates below are cumulative risks from birth to age five (deaths per live birth). The vaccines protect from the first doses at 6 weeks through the fifth birthday, about 4.9 years. The baseline is turned into an annual rate by dividing by this number and back into a cumulative risk by multiplying, so it cancels: it only keeps the template's per-year form and has no effect on the result.

rows.label: Measles deaths before age 5, per live birth (program zones)

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Appendix Table 2, under-5 CSMR, Measles row
source.quote: Measles 3.9 2.7 5.0 5.5 0.4 0.3 0.4 (national, NC, NE, NW, SE, SS, SW)

rows.explainer: Verbal-autopsy cause-specific death rate from the 2024 NDHS follow-up: 5.5 measles deaths per 1,000 live births in the North West and 5.0 in the North East (10 years before the survey), weighted 79/21 by 2024 enrolments (North West states Kano, Katsina, Jigawa, Sokoto, Kaduna, Kebbi and Zamfara enrolled 1,374,311 of 1,735,305 infants; Bauchi and Gombe in the North East 359,171; annual report 2024, p. 9): 5.4 per 1,000. The range reflects verbal-autopsy misclassification and measles' year-to-year swings (the low end is the national-level 3.9 rounded; the high end allows for under-attribution to measles of deaths labelled pneumonia or sepsis).

rows.label: Measles vaccine effectiveness, one dose at 9 months

source.title: Uzicanin & Zimmerman 2011, Field effectiveness of live attenuated measles-containing vaccines: a review of published literature, J Infect Dis 204(S1)
source.page: Abstract (read via Europe PMC)
source.quote: Seventy papers with 135 VE point estimates were identified.

rows.explainer: Median effectiveness of one dose given at 9–11 months was 77% across 135 estimates (interquartile range 62–91%), 84% in studies with verified vaccination and laboratory-confirmed measles; estimates were lower in the African region. Best 77%; range 62–88% (roughly the interquartile range). Nigeria's second routine dose (15 months) and campaigns are not credited here.

rows.label: Pertussis deaths before age 5, per live birth (program zones)

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Figures 3 and 4 (national cause-specific rates and counts by age group)
source.quote: vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, pertussis, and meningitis contribute substantially (9%) to under-5 mortality

rows.explainer: The zonal table groups pertussis under "other causes", so we start from the national rates: 0.9 pertussis deaths per 1,000 live births among post-neonates (7,551 deaths a year) and 1.4 among children 12–59 months (10,776 deaths), 2.3 in all. Scaled by the program zones' under-5 mortality (0.79 × 140 + 0.21 × 127 = 137 per 1,000) over the national 110: 2.9 per 1,000. Low end: national rate unscaled; high end 3.3 per 1,000 (1.45 × national, a modest step above the zones' all-cause ratio of 1.25). Verbal autopsy may misclassify: a 3% pertussis share at 12–59 months is high for a disease that kills mostly young infants, another reason not to go higher.

rows.label: Pentavalent (whole-cell pertussis) vaccine effectiveness against pertussis death

source.title: Fulton et al. 2016, Protective effect of contemporary pertussis vaccines: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Clin Infect Dis
source.page: Abstract (read via Europe PMC)
source.quote: overall wP vaccine effectiveness of 94% (95% CI, 88%-97%)

rows.explainer: Nigeria's pentavalent vaccine has a whole-cell pertussis component. The meta-analysis gives 94% for whole-cell vaccines; an older review (Jefferson et al. 2003, Vaccine) found absolute efficacy of whole-cell DTP ranging from 37% to 92% by product. Best 85% allows for weaker products, cold-chain failures and children who get fewer than three doses; low 60% follows the weaker products, high 94% the meta-analysis.

rows.label: Pneumococcal and Hib deaths before age 5, per live birth (program zones)

source.title: Wahl et al. 2018, Burden of Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae type b disease in children in the era of conjugate vaccines: global, regional, and national estimates for 2000–15, Lancet Glob Health
source.page: Abstract (read via Europe PMC)

rows.explainer:
Wahl et al. estimate 49,000 pneumococcal and 3,600 Hib deaths among Nigerian children aged 1–59 months in 2015, about 7 per 1,000 of the roughly 7.5 million births that year. Scaling to the program zones (under-5 mortality 137 vs 110 nationally) and to the decline in child mortality since 2015 (about 15%) gives about 7.5 per 1,000.

Cross-check from the 2024 verbal autopsy for the program zones: pneumonia after the first month 8.6, meningitis 3.4 and "sepsis" 23.8 per 1,000 (child share of each from the national age split); 40% of pneumonia, 50% of meningitis and 10% of the sepsis deaths being pneumococcal or Hib also gives 7.5 per 1,000. Best 8.5 per 1,000: a little above the burden models (7.5), giving the only mortality trial some weight, giving the only mortality trial some weight, discounted because The Gambia's pneumococcal burden was high and the trial covered ages 6 weeks–29 months only. Low 5 per 1,000 (Wahl's lower bound, scaled). High 12 per 1,000: the Gambian PCV trial found the vaccine cut all-cause child mortality by 16% (95% CI 3–28%; Cutts et al. 2005). Applied to the program zones' mortality after the first month (roughly 90 per 1,000), that is about 10–14 deaths prevented per 1,000 vaccinated children, against the 4.7 per 1,000 this model's pneumococcal/Hib chain prevents (burden × 56% × age share), so the trial points to a larger burden than either estimate.

rows.label: Share of pneumococcal and Hib deaths prevented by full PCV and pentavalent vaccination

source.title: Cutts et al. 2005, Efficacy of nine-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine against pneumonia and invasive pneumococcal disease in The Gambia, Lancet
source.page: Abstract (read via Europe PMC)
source.quote: We also found an efficacy of 16% (3-28) against mortality

rows.explainer: The Gambian trial found 77% (51–90%) efficacy against invasive disease from vaccine serotypes and 50% (21–69%) against invasive disease from all serotypes. Pneumococcal deaths are 93% of the pneumococcal-plus-Hib total (Wahl et al.); we use about 54% for pneumococcus (between the all-serotype 50% and vaccine-type coverage of about 70% × 77%) and about 90% for Hib (pentavalent), weighted: 56%. Low 40% (all-serotype efficacy's lower half), high 70% (PCV13 covering more serotypes than the trial's PCV9).

rows.label: Diarrhoea deaths before age 5, per live birth (program zones)

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Appendix Table 2, under-5 CSMR, Diarrhoea row
source.quote: Diarrhoea 7 3.3 10.2 8.8 5.0 2.5 1.3 (national, NC, NE, NW, SE, SS, SW)

rows.explainer: 8.8 per 1,000 live births in the North West and 10.2 in the North East, weighted by enrolments: 9.1 per 1,000. Low end: national 7.0; high end: the North East rate.

rows.label: Share of diarrhoea deaths prevented by full rotavirus vaccination

source.title: Jonesteller et al. 2017, Effectiveness of rotavirus vaccination: a systematic review of the first decade of global postlicensure data, Clin Infect Dis
source.page: Abstract (read via Europe PMC)
source.quote: median RV1 vaccine effectiveness (VE) of 84%, 75%, and 57% in countries with low, medium, and high child mortality

rows.explainer: Nigeria added rotavirus vaccine (ROTAVAC, at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, the same visits as pentavalent) from August 2022, starting with northern states (Gavi announcement), so it is part of what an incentivised visit delivers in 2024. Rotavirus caused about 128,500 under-5 deaths worldwide in 2016 (Troeger et al. 2018, JAMA Pediatrics), about 29% of diarrhoea deaths; times 57% effectiveness in high-mortality countries gives 17%. Troeger et al. also estimate wider use of the vaccine could have prevented about 20% of all diarrhoea deaths. Range 10–25%.

rows.label: Deaths before age 5 that full vaccination prevents, per live birth, population average
rows.formula: csmr_measles * ve_measles + csmr_pertussis * ve_pertussis + deaths_pneumo_hib * ve_pneumo_hib + csmr_diarrhoea * rota_preventable_share
rows.explainer: Deaths from each vaccine-preventable cause times the share the vaccine prevents, at the coverage of the period the death rates were measured (population averages, which include vaccinated children). Context only: the next rows correct it for protective age, mortality trend and the risk of an unvaccinated child. Not counted (they go to the unmodelled adjustment): tuberculosis (BCG), diphtheria, yellow fever, meningitis A, polio, hepatitis B.

rows.label: Child mortality in 2024–2029 relative to the verbal-autopsy reference period
rows.explainer: The zonal verbal-autopsy rates average the 10 years before the 2024 NDHS (midpoint about 2019), but the 2024 cohort is at risk in 2024–2029. National under-5 mortality fell from 132 (2018 NDHS) to 110 per 1,000 (2024 NDHS), about 3% a year (NVASA policy brief, Figure 1); the North West fell less, and its zero-dose share rose between 2021 and 2024. A decline of about 1.5% a year over the ~7 years between the reference midpoint and the cohort's at-risk period gives 0.9. Low 0.8 (national pace continues); high 1.0 (no decline in the north). Applied to the verbal-autopsy causes only; the pneumococcal/Hib burden is already scaled to today (deaths_pneumo_hib).

rows.label: Share of measles deaths at ages the 9-month dose protects

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Figure 4 and Appendix Table 1 (cause-specific deaths by age group)
source.quote: N = 327,261  N = 175,604  N = 399,099 (neonates, post-neonates, children 12-59 months)

rows.explainer: Nationally 4,566 of 29,709 under-5 measles deaths (15%) are at 1–11 months and 25,143 at 12–59 months. Infants dying of measles at 9–11 months can be protected by the dose at 9 months, younger ones cannot. Best 90% at protectable ages (about two thirds of the infant measles deaths taken as before 9 months); range 85–95%.

rows.label: Share of pertussis deaths at ages the pentavalent series protects

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Figure 4 and Appendix Table 1 (cause-specific deaths by age group)
source.quote: N = 327,261  N = 175,604  N = 399,099 (neonates, post-neonates, children 12-59 months)

rows.explainer: Nationally 7,551 pertussis deaths are at 1–11 months and 10,776 at 12–59 months (41% infants). Infant pertussis deaths cluster before the third dose at 14 weeks, though the first and second doses already give partial protection. Best 85%; low 75% (most infant deaths unprotectable), high 92%.

rows.label: Share of pneumococcal, Hib and rotavirus deaths at ages the vaccines protect
rows.explainer: Pneumococcal, Hib and rotavirus deaths are spread over infancy and early childhood (Wahl et al. count ages 1–59 months); deaths in the first 6–10 weeks, before the first doses take effect, are a small share. Best 95%, range 90–100%.

rows.label: Measles: unvaccinated child's risk relative to population average
rows.explainer: Population death rates mix vaccinated and unvaccinated children: average risk = (1 − c × e) of an unvaccinated child's, for coverage c and effectiveness e in the period the rate was measured. Measles coverage in the north was around 35–40% over the reference period (New Incentives' baseline surveys found 61% zero-dose) and e ≈ 0.77, so 1/(1 − 0.29) ≈ 1.4. Low 1.2 (the children the incentive brings in are less at risk than the never-vaccinated); high 1.6 (unvaccinated children are poorer and farther from care). The 2023–24 NDHS (Key Indicators Report PR157, Table 15) gives, for children 12–23 months, measles 37.2%, DPT-HepB-Hib 3 39.7% and no vaccinations 46.6% in the North West; measles 53.6% in the North East. Weighted 79/21 that is about 41% measles coverage today, a little higher than over the reference period.

rows.label: Pertussis: unvaccinated child's risk relative to population average
rows.explainer: As for measles, with three-dose pentavalent coverage of roughly a quarter to a third in the north over the reference period (lower than first-dose coverage; zero-dose about half) and e ≈ 0.85: 1/(1 − 0.24) ≈ 1.3. Range 1.15–1.5 for the same reasons. The 2023–24 NDHS (Key Indicators Report PR157, Table 15) gives, for children 12–23 months, measles 37.2%, DPT-HepB-Hib 3 39.7% and no vaccinations 46.6% in the North West; measles 53.6% in the North East.

rows.label: Pneumococcal/Hib: unvaccinated child's risk relative to the 2015-based burden
rows.explainer: The pneumococcal/Hib burden is from Wahl et al. for 2015, the first full year of Nigeria's phased PCV introduction, when PCV coverage in the north was very low and Hib (pentavalent) coverage low too. So the population figure is close to an unvaccinated child's risk. Best 1.05, range 1.0–1.2. Rotavirus gets no multiplier (1.0): the vaccine reached the north only in August 2022, after most of the verbal-autopsy reference period.

rows.label: Vaccine-preventable deaths before age 5 for an unvaccinated child, per birth, 2024 cohort
rows.formula: mortality_trend_adj * (csmr_measles * ve_measles * share_after_protection_measles * risk_mult_measles + csmr_pertussis * ve_pertussis * share_after_protection_pertussis * risk_mult_pertussis + csmr_diarrhoea * rota_preventable_share * share_after_protection_other) + deaths_pneumo_hib * ve_pneumo_hib * share_after_protection_other * risk_mult_pneumo_hib
rows.explainer: Per cause: death rate × share the vaccine prevents × share of deaths at protectable ages × unvaccinated-child multiplier, with the verbal-autopsy causes scaled to the 2024–2029 mortality level. About 1.3% of an unvaccinated child's births end in a death full vaccination would have prevented, roughly a tenth of the zones' under-5 mortality (about 137 per 1,000).

rows.label: Annual vaccine-preventable mortality of an unvaccinated child under 5
rows.explainer: Cumulative vaccine-preventable risk to age five for an unvaccinated child in the program zones (vpd_risk_unvaccinated), spread over the 4.9 years at risk.

rows.label: Increase in vaccination among all children in served areas (randomised trial)

source.title: IDinsight, Impact of Conditional Cash Transfers on Routine Childhood Immunizations: Evidence from North West Nigeria (evaluation brief)
source.page: p. 3, Figure 1

rows.explainer:
Cluster-randomised trial in 167 clinic catchments in Katsina, Zamfara and Jigawa (2017–2020), surveying 5,173 children aged 12–16 months. The program raised coverage of BCG by 16 points (95% CI 12–21), Penta 1 by 21 (16–26), Measles 1 by 14 (10–18) and full immunisation by 27 (23–32), from about 25% in control areas. Non-incentivised vaccines given at the same visits rose by similar amounts (Hep B 16, IPV 18, yellow fever 18).

We need one gain weighted by where the deaths are: measles is about a third of the deaths averted (gain 14 points); pentavalent, PCV and rotavirus (three-dose series) about two thirds, with a gain a little above Penta 1's 21 points, say 22: part of the 27-point full-immunisation gain is children moving from partial to full schedules who already had partial protection. Weighted: 0.34 × 14 + 0.66 × 22 ≈ 19 points. Low: the measles gain (14); high: the full-immunisation gain (27).

At scale, New Incentives' before/after surveys in nine expansion cohorts (2024 coverage report) found Penta 1 up 25 points (95% CI 22–29), Measles 1 up 18 (14–22) and zero-dose down 26 points after 24 months; these are pre-post, not randomised, but consistent with the trial.

rows.label: Share of children born in served catchments whom the program enrols
rows.explainer: The trial effect is per child living in a served catchment, but the cost is per infant enrolled. If only a share of catchment children ever enrol, each enrolment carries 1/share of the effect. New Incentives' surveys 24 months after rollout found 68% of 6–12-month-olds with BCG, 65% with Penta 1 and 35% zero-dose; only children who visit a clinic can enrol, so roughly two thirds to three quarters of children enrol. Cross-check: 2024 North West enrolments (1,374,311) equal 66% of all North West births (2,091,409; NVASA policy brief, Appendix Table 2), and New Incentives is not in every clinic, so the share within served catchments must be at least about two thirds. Best 75%; low 65% (that floor); high 95% (enrolment counts include children from outside the surveyed areas, and the trial's catchment boundaries were drawn more widely than the program's enrolment base).

rows.label: Share of enrolled infants vaccinated because of the incentive
rows.explainer: The trial's coverage gain per catchment child divided by the share of catchment children who enrol: the probability that an enrolled infant is a child the incentive moved from unvaccinated to vaccinated. Multiplied by the vaccine-preventable risk above, it is the reduction in mortality per enrolled infant.

rows.label: Deaths averted per infant enrolled (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Unvaccinated child's vaccine-preventable risk to age five × share of enrollees the incentive gets vaccinated. Roughly 1 death averted per 300 infants enrolled before adjustments.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted that are of children under five

source.title: 2024 Nigeria Verbal Autopsy and Social Autopsy Study, Policy Brief No. 1
source.page: Appendix Table 2 (under-5 cause-specific mortality rates)

rows.explainer: All deaths counted come from under-five cause-specific death rates, so all are valued at GiveWell's under-five weight. Deaths averted after age five (measles and pertussis protection lasting beyond the fifth birthday) are not counted here; they are part of the unmodelled adjustment.

rows.label: Illness averted per infant enrolled (years lived with disability)

source.title: Not modelled separately: see unmodelled_benefits_adj
source.page: n/a

rows.explainer: Set to 0: non-fatal illness averted (measles complications, pneumonia episodes, meningitis sequelae such as deafness, rotavirus hospitalisations) is counted in unmodelled_benefits_adj instead, so it is not counted twice.

rows.label: Later-life income gain per infant enrolled, ln(consumption) units, present value

source.title: No direct evidence for this program; see unmodelled_benefits_adj
source.page: p. 6, recommendations (further research on indirect effects)

rows.explainer: Set to 0: there is no direct evidence on later-life income from childhood vaccination of the kind available for malaria or deworming. A possible developmental benefit of avoided illness is included in the unmodelled adjustment. The value of the cash itself to households is modelled separately (uov_cash).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Three parts. (1) The trial: a well-powered cluster-randomised trial of this very program, but a single trial, with caregiver-reported outcomes (cross-checked against cards and registers); caregivers in treated areas may over-report vaccination more: about 0.9. (2) Carrying it to 2024: ten states instead of three, 6,500 clinics instead of 84, and an incentive whose dollar value fell with the naira (₦4,000 ≈ $11 in 2019; ₦11,000 including the new completion bonus ≈ $7 in 2024, roughly similar in local purchasing power). The before/after surveys in nine expansion cohorts show gains of the same size, which supports external validity, though they are not randomised: about 0.9. (3) The mortality chain rests on verbal-autopsy causes of death and on vaccine efficacy from other settings, not on a mortality trial of the program; the ranges of those inputs carry most of that, so a small further discount for model error: about 0.92. Product ≈ 0.75. Low 0.55: the trial overstates and scale dilutes; high 0.95: the trial's effect holds at scale. Reference: the at-scale before/after surveys find full-vaccination (strict) gains of about 17–22 points against the trial's 27 (ratio about 0.7–0.8), which is the external-validity anchor; internal/external validity discounts on single-RCT programs in evaluator models are typically 0.6–0.9.

rows.label: Share of the extra vaccinations that would not have happened later anyway
rows.explainer: The trial measured coverage at 12–16 months against a control group that already reflects the government's own efforts (control coverage rose between baseline and endline). Measles, yellow fever and IPV campaigns ran in the study areas just before endline (IDinsight brief, p. 4), but the brief also says "any injectable vaccine" coverage was similar across arms partly because of those campaigns, so it is unclear whether campaign doses were counted in the routine "Measles 1" outcome; if they were not, the measured measles gain overstates the protection gained. On top of that comes catch-up after 16 months (routine visits at older ages, later campaigns such as the post-COVID "Big Catch-Up"), although late vaccination leaves the first year, when risk is highest, unprotected. Best 85% overall (about 75% for measles, which is a third of the deaths averted, and 90% for the infant series); low 65% if campaigns and catch-up reach most of the children the incentive brings in; high 100% if late catch-up is negligible (North West zero-dose was 46.6% in the 2023–24 NDHS). We did not find a catch-up table to anchor this further.

rows.label: Government and Gavi cost of fully vaccinating one extra child
rows.explainer: The extra vaccinations use vaccines, syringes, cold chain and clinic staff paid by the Nigerian government and Gavi. PCV alone costs $2.05–3.30 a dose under the Gavi/AMC price (UNICEF Supply Division PCV price data, updated June 2026; https://www.unicef.org/supply/media/25651/file/PCV-vaccine-prices-17062026.pdf), so three doses are about $9; add three rotavirus doses, three pentavalent, IPV, measles, BCG and yellow fever, wastage from multi-dose vials, and a little staff time at sessions that run anyway: about $20. Low $10 (vaccines only, little wastage); high $35 (more wastage and delivery cost). UNICEF's 2024 standard-cost note for fully vaccinating a child sat behind a bot check and was not read.

rows.label: New Incentives' share of the cost of the extra vaccinations
rows.explainer: Following the house convention that co-funders' costs lower the attribution share rather than entering cost_total: per infant enrolled, New Incentives spends cost_per_person and the government and Gavi spend the cost of vaccinating the extra children the incentive brings in (share vaccinated because of the incentive × cost per child). New Incentives is credited with its share of that total, about three quarters.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: With full credit for shared outcomes switched on, New Incentives gets the whole outcome.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (enrolment counts that are real and new)
rows.explainer: The enrolment count is administrative. Duplicate or fictitious enrolments (cash creates an incentive to game them) and infants enrolled in more than one clinic would inflate it. New Incentives runs unannounced audits of 13% of disbursement sessions (annual report 2024, p. 18) and its program data show 95% of enrolled infants reaching Penta 1 and 86% measles, consistent with real children. The trial effect already reflects real-world delivery, so this only covers the count. Best 0.95; low 0.85; high 1.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Governments and other agencies don't fund incentives in these areas, so classic funging is unlikely. But New Incentives holds large reserves relative to its spending: net assets of $89.5 million at the end of 2024 against $25.7 million of expenses and $11.5 million of support (audited statements, p. 5), and it raises a 2–3-year runway before entering an area (annual report, p. 21). A marginal donation therefore mostly extends the runway or brings forward later expansion rather than adding infants this year, and a few large funders supply most of its money and might fill gaps. Best 0.9; low 0.7 (the money mostly sits in reserves for years); high 1.05 if the program's results lead governments to adopt or co-fund incentives. For comparison, GiveWell-imported models on this site carry leverage/funging discounts of roughly 8% (SMC) to 31% (vitamin A).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits and costs not modelled, as a share of modelled health value
rows.explainer: Applied to the value of deaths averted only (the cash is modelled separately). Positive: non-fatal illness averted (measles, pneumonia, meningitis sequelae, rotavirus) +8%; herd protection of unenrolled children from measles and PCV, and fewer stockouts benefiting unenrolled children at served clinics (the stockout effect on enrolled children is already in the trial's coverage gain), +5%; vaccines given at the same visits but not modelled (BCG, IPV, hepatitis B, yellow fever, meningitis A; diphtheria returned to northern Nigeria in 2023) +5%; deaths averted after age five +2%; possible developmental and income gains from avoided illness +5%. Negative: caregivers' time and travel to clinics, and pressure on crowded sessions, −2%. Sum about 23%; low 10%, high 45%.

rows.label: Deaths averted
Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights for the age mix of deaths averted (all under five here), times your multiplier on the value of a life.

rows.label: Units of value from deaths averted
Units of value from illness averted
rows.explainer: Zero here: illness averted is in the unmodelled adjustment.

rows.label: Units of value from later-life income
rows.explainer: Zero here: no direct evidence; see ln_income_gain_per_person.

rows.label: Cash paid to caregivers, 2024

source.title: New Incentives and Subsidiary, audited consolidated financial statements, years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023
source.page: p. 7, Consolidated Statement of Functional Expenses, 2024

rows.explainer: The incentives themselves, about $4.88 per infant enrolled (the annual report gives ₦12.7 billion disbursed in 8.7 million payments). This money reaches poor caregivers and has value of its own, separate from the vaccinations it buys.

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption)-years per dollar of cash received by a poor household
rows.explainer: Anchored on GiveDirectly, the site's benchmark: its model on this site gives about 0.0086 units of value per dollar donated; with roughly 80–85% of its spending reaching recipients that is about 0.01 units per dollar received, i.e. 0.01 / 1.4427 ≈ 0.0069 ln-consumption-years per dollar received (one unit of value = 1/ln 2 = 1.4427 ln-units). Caregivers in rural northern Nigeria are at least as poor as GiveDirectly's recipients, which pushes this up; the payments are small and spread over a year, which may make them less valuable than lump sums for investment. We have not sourced the share of GiveDirectly's spending that reaches recipients, and a direct check points lower: $1 is a much smaller share of a northern Nigerian household's annual consumption per person (a few hundred dollars at market rates) than ln-utility would need for 0.0069, unless that consumption is under $150 a year. Best 0.006 (between the two), low 0.0035, high 0.0104. Converted to units of value with the shared $uov_per_ln_consumption, so the cash branch moves with GiveDirectly when a visitor changes that assumption.

rows.label: Units of value from the cash itself
rows.explainer: Cash paid, scaled to the full 2024 cohort like the cost, times its consumption value, with the same leverage/funging discount as the health value (a marginal donation partly extends the runway). Not discounted for evidence or attribution: the cash is paid whatever the vaccination effect. A deliberate extension of the direct-health template: the cash transfer is part of this program's outcome.

rows.label: Total units of value
rows.explainer: Health value with the unmodelled-benefits allowance, plus the value of the cash (a branch added to the direct-health template's outcome formula because the incentive itself is a transfer to poor households).

Salaries, benefits, taxes and consultants, 2024

rows.explainer: Total staff and consultant pay across program, management and fundraising.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: About 34% of 2024 spending; most of it pays some 3,400 Nigerian field staff.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: Most of the pay goes to locally hired field officers in northern Nigeria, for whom a salaried NGO job is usually at or above local private-sector alternatives; a smaller share goes to management in Nigeria and the US, who likely earn less than they could elsewhere. Best 5%, below the repo's 15% reference for large delivery charities because the staff mix is so heavily local field staff; low 0, high 15% (the delivery-charity reference).
